title: 10 Detroit Lions to watch in preseason Game 2 vs. Commanders
summary: There’s just over a week until the Detroit Lions—and every other NFL team—must cut their roster down to 53 players. That makes Saturday afternoon’s preseason game between the Lions and Washington Commanders an important one. For many, this will be one of the final chances to not only impress their own team, but put out […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive end Derrick Moore (9) practices during mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co There’s just over a week until the Detroit Lions—and every other NFL team—must cut their roster down to 53 players. That makes Saturday afternoon’s preseason game between the Lions and Washington Commanders an important one. For many, this will be one of the final chances to not only impress their own team, but put out good tape for other teams to find. So here are 10 players to keep an eye on during Saturday’s game. QB Josh Dobbs The Lions typically prefer to have a veteran backup quarterback, so you’d think Josh Dobbs would be the favorite to win the job, despite only being added to the roster less than two weeks ago. But Dobbs has not gotten much playing time during practice or the preseason, so it’s hard to know where he stands. Coach Dan Campbell said Dobbs will get the start on Saturday, giving him a chance to play with some starters and make a strong impression. Can he do enough to keep undrafted rookie Luke Altmyer at bay? RB Sione Vaki Vaki’s roster spot is not really in question due to his special teams value, but the Lions have been trying to develop him as a running back since they drafted him two seasons ago. Unfortunately, injuries have limited his ability to get reps, but Saturday is finally a chance to bank some running back snaps and show off his progress. WR Tay Martin Martin has been the biggest riser midway through camp. Both Campbell and special teams coordinator Dave Fipp have raved about his special teams skills, but can he make an impact on offense? With no clear leader for the WR5 and/or WR6 jobs, Martin has a chance to make a statement—as do Dominic Lovett, Cedrick Wilson, and Tom Kennedy. The entire starting offensive line It’s unclear how many starters will end up playing on Saturday, but if I were Dan Campbell, I’d at least give every starting offensive lineman a series or two. With the shuffling of lineups—particularly on the interior—the chemistry is still clearly not where it needs to be. So Campbell would be wise to use this opportunity to get those valuable snaps in. Any sign of progress when it comes to chemistry would be welcome, especially with expected starter Juice Scruggs now finally ramping up to a full set of snaps each practice. I suspect he’ll split time with Seth McLaughlin—and I wouldn’t be surprised if Penei Sewell sits entirely—but the more reps built with the offensive line, the better. EDGE Derrick Moore Moore has missed a bunch of camp with an injury, but he returned this past week and made an impact immediately. The rookie second-round pick could make his preseason debut on Saturday, and how he performs against the Commanders could go a long way in determining how much of a role he’ll have out of the gate. DT Ben Stille Stille has a long road to go to win a roster spot, but he’s a player who has seemingly made a play every day in camp over the last couple of weeks. Capable of playing anywhere from the nose to the big end spot, Stille’s disruptive play at camp has him officially on my sleepers list . Could he work his way onto the roster bubble and upset someone like Levi Onwuzurike for a roster spot? I’m not counting it out completely. LB Devin White vs. LB Malcolm Rodriguez There’s quietly a starting competition at play at the linebacker level. Malcolm Rodriguez had what seemed like a pretty strong hold on the starting WILL linebacker job, but then he suffered an ankle injury, missed about a week of practice, and the Lions signed Devin White. Since then, it’s mostly been White with the starters and Rodriguez working his way back with the second-team defense. I believe this remains a battle, and how both perform against the Commanders could shift the dynamics as Detroit enters the final week of training camp. LB Erick Hunter Hunter has been the most talked-about UDFA rookie, and for a good reason. He consistently makes plays on special teams, and flashes on defense as well. Lions special teams coordinator Dave Fipp simultaneously praised Hunter while also preaching caution due to his frequent mistakes. A small-school player may need to develop for a year on the practice squad, but if Hunter balls out Saturday, he may make the Lions think twice about subjecting him to waivers. CB Keith Abney Over the past week, Abney has slowly worked his way into the starting nickel conversation. He’s split time with Christian Izien with the starters, which has been a good experience for the rookie fifth-round pick. He’s still clearly adjusting to the nickel position, but Saturday should be a big opportunity for him to go up against a fairly talented Commanders receiving corps (Stefon Diggs, Terry McLaurin, and Luke McCaffrey). S Dan Jackson Thomas Harper missed last practice. At this point, there’s no clear reason for his absence, but if he can’t go on Saturday, Dan Jackson is likely to get a ton of playing time. Detroit would be wise not to subject Avonte Maddox and Chuck Clark—the two projected Week 1 starters—to too much playing time, leaving just Jackson and Aamaris Brown to play for the remainder of the game. Jackson seemed destined for a four-core special teams role last year before a preseason injury derailed his rookie season. And he’s so far down the depth chart right now that he needs a standout preseason performance to work his way back into the conversation.

title: Detroit Lions updated depth chart: Preseason Game 2 vs. Commanders
summary: Ahead of every Detroit Lions game in 2026, we will provide readers with an updated depth chart of the team’s roster based on what we are seeing at practices, with this installment representing where we believe the Lions roster sits heading into preseason Game 2 against the Washington Commanders. In the Lions first presesason game against the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14), center right, practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, August 10, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Ahead of every Detroit Lions game in 2026, we will provide readers with an updated depth chart of the team’s roster based on what we are seeing at practices, with this installment representing where we believe the Lions roster sits heading into preseason Game 2 against the Washington Commanders. In the Lions first presesason game against the Bengals, they rested 32 players (including 18 starters) along with another three on injury lists (PUP/NFI). However, Campbell has previously stated that the plan is to play some Lions starters in this upcoming game , but with six practices in the last seven days, including multiple padded and a full-team scrimmage , he also noted those plans could change. Meeks looks like the current leader for the Lions TE4 role, but he’ll need to stay sharp, especially under the lights. The Lions will be televised live locally on all of the Detroit Lions TV Network affiliates. In the metro Detroit area, that’s Fox 2 Detroit. For other affiliates, check the Lions’ map here . Is it being replayed nationally? Yes, NFL Network is replaying the game on Sunday, August 23 at 3:30 a.m. ET. So… you may want to DVR it. Can I stream the game? Yes! If you are not a local Lions fan, you can watch the game on NFL+ with a subscription. Local fans can watch the game on DetroitLions.com or via the official Lions app for free! Who is playing in the Lions vs. Commanders? Dan Campbell said that he plans on playing a significant amount of his starters, but he wouldn’t expand upon that. We also know Jared Goff won’t play, and Josh Dobbs will start at quarterback. As for the Commanders, “a good amount” of starters will play vs. the Lions . title: Packers Discussion: Should Tyrod Taylor or Kyle McCord be the backup QB?
summary: Alright, I’m clearing the lane here so you guys can sound off on what you think about the Green Bay Packers’ backup quarterback job in 2026. It’s a bit of a lightning rod topic, so let’s just set the table and recap how we ended up in the position that we’re at right now. Green […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Kyle McCord #18 of the Green Bay Packers warms up before the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Alright, I’m clearing the lane here so you guys can sound off on what you think about the Green Bay Packers’ backup quarterback job in 2026. It’s a bit of a lightning rod topic, so let’s just set the table and recap how we ended up in the position that we’re at right now. Green Bay’s backup last year was Malik Willis, who signed a three-year, $67.5 million contract with the Miami Dolphins this offseason that should earn the Packers a third-round compensatory pick in 2027 . The practice squad quarterback last year was Clayton Tune, who was left for dead in the junior varsity game against the Minnesota Vikings to end the 2025 regular season and was later replaced by Desmond Ridder, who was signed on New Year’s Eve, in the playoffs. After the Packers’ playoff loss to the Chicago Bears, the team signed both Ridder and Kyle McCord, a 2025 draft pick who spent his rookie season on the Philadelphia Eagles’ practice squad, to reserve/futures contracts (essentially the minimum deals that practice squadders usually receive). Post-draft, Green Bay signed rookie Kyron Drones, who was cut after a Week 1 preseason performance where he dropped back four times and was sacked three times, including once on a screen. Three days after the Drones signing, Ridder was swapped out for veteran Tyrod Taylor, who is on a one-year, $2.5 million contract with another $2.5 million in (mostly unlikely to be earned) incentives for playing time, regular-season wins and a playoff berth with him under center. If the Packers chose to release Taylor now, they’d be charged $700,000 on the salary cap this year, compared to his current cap hit of $2.9 million, according to Spotrac . If Taylor makes the roster in Week 1, though, as a vested veteran, then his $1.3 million base salary will be fully guaranteed for the year, meaning that Green Bay would be on the hook for it, whether or not they decide to cut Taylor at a later date. None of that salary was previously guaranteed, as the only guaranteed money in his deal came in the form of a $700,000 signing bonus. Here’s the hitch: McCord has clearly outplayed Taylor in the preseason. We all have eyes. We all see it. Maybe Taylor is just having some bad throws in the preseason, and he looks better in practice, but it hasn’t looked good against the Pittsburgh Steelers and Denver Broncos. Right now, McCord is currently sixth in the NFL this preseason in passing yards with 220. That list includes Carolina’s Kenny Pickett, who ranks ahead of McCord but also got to play in the Hall of Fame Game before Weeks 1 and 2 of the preseason. Overall, McCord has gone 24 for 35 (69 percent) for 220 yards (6.3 yards per attempt) and orchestrated three two-minute drills at the end of first halves over two games. Yes, he did it twice in a single game (against Denver on Friday). He’s not making the most difficult wow throws imaginable, but he’s hitting out routes with timing and moving the chains while showing a little bravery and composure in the pocket. Meanwhile, Taylor is 8 of 16 (50 percent) for 38 yards (2.4 yards per attempt) and has a long of seven yards over two games. Yes, he has 38 yards over 34 offensive snaps . The third-team offense has moved the ball noticeably better than the second-team offense, particularly in the air. Passing game coordinator Jason Vrable, who was a coach in Buffalo when Taylor was a part of the team, said today that the 37-year-old still has the same arm strength that he had back in the day , but I’m not sure fans are convinced of that after watching some of the floating Taylor incompletions in Denver. After McCord’s performance against the Broncos, it feels like the first time all summer that the backup quarterback job behind Jordan Love is potentially up for grabs. Hell, a week ago McCord was still battling Drones for the third quarterback job. Now, there’s a real chance that McCord might be the backup, depending on how the two perform against the Arizona Cardinals in the preseason finale. For what it’s worth, head coach Matt LaFleur has stated that the plan this week is for the starters to get work in the team’s joint practice against the Cardinals, coached by LaFleur’s younger brother, while the preseason game will mostly be used to evaluate backups. So we’ll get a deeper look into both Taylor and McCord this upcoming week. How are you feeling about the backup quarterback job right now, and what would you do? Roll with Taylor? Swap Taylor out with McCord? Buy a different veteran still on the street like Jimmy Garoppolo? Sound off in the comments section. Join the conversation! title: Green Bay Packers Roster: Post-Preseason Week 2 53-man projection
summary: After Week 2’s action against the Denver Broncos, we did a full breakdown of the Green Bay Packers’ entire depth chart, position-by-position, while showing our work. Now we’re going to take it a step further and update our 53-man roster projection with our best guess on what the team will look like when the club […]
full_text: Kamal Hadden #36 of the Green Bay Packers holds a football during training camp at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images After Week 2’s action against the Denver Broncos, we did a full breakdown of the Green Bay Packers’ entire depth chart , position-by-position, while showing our work. Now we’re going to take it a step further and update our 53-man roster projection with our best guess on what the team will look like when the club announces that they’ve successfully dropped 38 players from the 91-man offseason roster. Quarterback Jordan Love Tyrod Taylor Yes, Kyle McCord has clearly been outplaying Tyrod Taylor in the preseason so far, but Taylor is still taking all of the second-team snaps, while McCord only received all of the outright third-team snaps following the release of Kyron Drones last week. I don’t think the door is completely closed on McCord winning the job, or the team pivoting to a veteran option like Jimmy Garoppolo, but right now I’m guessing that Taylor is the backup in Week 1. Running Back Josh Jacobs MarShawn Lloyd Chris Brooks Barring injury or suspension, it’s going to be tough for Pierre Strong Jr., the Packers’ fourth running back option, to make the roster. He will probably be a practice squad priority for them, though, and be called up if Green Bay is ever down a body at the position. Receiver Christian Watson Matthew Golden Jayden Reed Savion Williams Bo Melton Skyy Moore J. Michael Sturdivant The top six are essentially roster locks as far as I see it. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are the team’s starting outside receivers, while Jayden Reed continues to start as a slot-exclusive player for Green Bay. Savion Williams is Watson’s direct backup, Bo Melton is Golden’s direct backup and Skyy Moore is Reed’s direct backup on offense. Beyond just offense, Williams has been getting work as a kick returner and punt gunner, Melton has been getting work as a punt gunner and jammer on the punt return team and Moore has been getting work as a kick and punt returner. All three of the backup receivers have special teams ability, which helps their situations. The final roster spot here I’m giving to J. Michael Sturdivant, who is also being onboarded to play some key special teams roles (punt gunner and lead blocker on punt return). Technically, Isaiah Neyor does seem to be one spot ahead of Sturdivant on the offensive depth chart, but I think the special teams ability (which helps Green Bay not only cover injuries at the receiver position but also at defensive back) gives Sturdivant a little boost. It’s possible that Sturdivant exited the Broncos game with a concussion, which sort of muddies this projection. We’ll learn more about Sturdivant’s status when the press asks head coach Matt LaFleur about it this week. Tight End Tucker Kraft Josh Whyle The Packers are good for one “roster game” every cutdown. I think this year, it could be at tight end. With Luke Musgrave (neck) still on the PUP list, I’m not sure Green Bay needs to worry about Drake Dabney or Messiah Swinson being picked up on waivers at the cutdown deadline. If the Packers drop to just two tight ends at initial cuts, as I’m projecting, they can hold an extra player for a day (or more) longer, hoping that they can more safely pass that player on the practice squad through waivers as other teams fill up their rosters. At worst, I think Green Bay can plan on calling up a Dabney or Swinson from the practice squad until Musgrave is activated. At best, maybe they add a tight end themselves via waivers. I fully expect the team to have three tight ends on the 46-man gameday roster against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 1. I just don’t necessarily think that means that three of them have to be on the initial roster at cutdowns. Offensive Line Zach Bako-Bewele (RT) Sean Rhyan (C) Jordan Morgan (LT) Aaron Banks (LG) Jacob Monk (G/C) Jager Burton (G/C) Anthony Belton (RT/RG) Donovan Jennings (G/C) John Williams (LT) Darian Kinnard (RT/RG) The player I’m most iffy about making this team is probably Donovan Jennings, but he continues to be rotated into the offensive line quickly in the preseason and is grading out decently — at least in line with the Packers’ other backup offensive linemen. If they only keep nine, I’m assuming that Jennings is the cut, but as of now I have 10 making the team. Defensive Line Devonte Wyatt Karl Brooks Javon Hargrave Warren Brinson Chris McClellan Jonathan Ford The roster squeeze is going to be felt the most on the interior defensive line, where Jonathan Ford, Nazir Stackhouse and Anthony Campbell are all fighting for essentially one roster spot. Right now, I’d give the nod to Ford, who has started back-to-back preseason games with the first-team defense as a head-up nose tackle. He has a more defined role in the starting lineup than either Stackhouse or Campbell at the moment. Reminder: Jordon Riley will start the year on the PUP list, too. Edge Defender Lukas Van Ness Barryn Sorrell Brenton Cox Jr. Collin Oliver Dani Dennis-Sutton This is a pretty clear 1-2-3-4 pecking order, with the question mark being where rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton, who has been held out of back-to-back preseason games after overheating in a practice, fits into the mix. Assume the early-season starters will be Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell, with Brenton Cox Jr. being the next man up and Collin Oliver playing in some obvious pass-rushing situations. Once Micah Parsons returns from the PUP list, the team might have to drop one of these players (if injuries haven’t already solved that problem), at which point they’ll need to ask themselves whether they believe holding Cox through the end of the 2026 season is more valuable than hanging onto the remainder of Oliver’s rookie contract. It’s likely that Arron Mosby makes the team’s practice squad and is called up at some point during the 2026 season to play special teams, but that’s mostly a kicking game thing, as he hasn’t contributed much as a defender in the NFL. Off-Ball Linebacker Zaire Franklin Edgerrin Cooper Isaiah McDuffie Ty’Ron Hopper Nick Niemann This one is pretty clear. They’re running back the unit from last year but replacing Quay Walker with Zaire Franklin. Kristian Welch should be available to call up from the practice squad if there are injuries, and he, like Nick Niemann, is mostly in Green Bay to play special teams, not defense. Cornerback Keisean Nixon Carrington Valentine Brandon Cisse Benjamin St-Juste Domani Jackson Domani Jackson actually worked behind Jaylin Simpson versus the Broncos, but Jackson also just returned to practice recently after recovering from an offseason surgery to his core. Brian Gutekunst doesn’t really like letting go of his draft picks, so I’m leaning Jackson here over Simpson. Safety Xavier McKinney Evan Williams Javon Bullard Kitan Oladapo Kamal Hadden The top four are pretty self-explanatory, as they’ve been on the roster since 2024, when they were all added to the team. Shoutout to whoever was doing safety crosschecks for the Packers that year. I’m moving Kamal Hadden to the safety position, as he only played the slot role and the third safety role for the Packers against the Broncos, displacing Kitan Oladapo as Javon Bullard’s preferred backup. With that being said, Oladapo plays the true safety position, too, which Hadden hasn’t done (at least yet). If you want to think about it this way: The backup at true safety would be Bullard (who would then kick to the slot when the team is not in their 3-4 base). When Bullard kicks to the slot if there were an injury to Xavier McKinney or Evan Williams, Oladapo would play that true safety role. If Bullard is ever hurt, Hadden would step up in the slot. That’s how the Packers are covering their bases right now. Kicker Trey Smack Punter Daniel Whelan Long Snapper Matt Orzech The Packers continue to hang onto Matt Orzech, which makes…

summary: The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman got the scoop on the Green Bay Packers’ injuries from the team’s victory over the Denver Broncos on Friday. According to Schneidman, five Packers suffered injuries last night. The first is cornerback Brandon Cisse, who we knew got banged up on special teams between the first and second drive of defense […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 23: Savion Williams #83 of the Green Bay Packers runs with the ball against the Minnesota Vikings during the first quarter at Lambeau Field on November 23, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman got the scoop on the Green Bay Packers’ injuries from the team’s victory over the Denver Broncos on Friday. According to Schneidman, five Packers suffered injuries last night. The first is cornerback Brandon Cisse , who we knew got banged up on special teams between the first and second drive of defense against Denver. After the game, Cisse stated that his knee injury was “ nothing serious ,” and Schneidman described the decision to keep Cisse out as “mostly precautionary.” Defensive lineman Warren Brinson injured his calf in warmups, which is why he didn’t play a single snap for the Packers on Friday , while also not being listed as a scratch for the game. Receiver J. Michael Sturdivant was evaluated for a concussion, but the diagnosis is unknown, per Schneidman. Here are the ones that weren’t caught by the broadcast team: Receiver Savion Williams injured his ankle, which is why he only played two offensive snaps (both with the first-team offense) yesterday. Edge rusher Collin Oliver has a calf injury, too. Oliver played six defensive snaps and seven special teams snaps versus the Broncos. For whatever it’s worth, we had all five of these injured players making Green Bay’s initial 53-man roster in our most recent projection , so losing any of them to a long-term injury would obviously have an influence on roster cutdowns. The next opportunity for the Packers to address these injuries will be before Monday’s practice. For what it’s worth, receiver Jayden Reed didn’t miss Friday’s game with an injury, but was out with a personal matter. — Update: Sports Illustrated ’s Bill Huber is reporting that Reed was at his grandmother’s funeral. Well wishes for the Reed family in this difficult time. Huber also said this: DT Devonte Wyatt: Wyatt was on the initial list of players who would not play. Instead, with Brinson a surprise scratch, he started and played four snaps. So it sounds like Wyatt might only have played because of Brinson’s injury. Interesting.

title: Trey Smack continues to pay off on Packers’ and fans’ faith
summary: For a second straight preseason game, the Green Bay Packers got a magnificent performance out of rookie kicker Trey Smack. In the Packers’ 33-13 win over the Denver Broncos on Friday night, Smack had another perfect night, hitting all four of his field goal attempts. Similarly to his debut in Pittsburgh, Smack also booted a […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - AUGUST 21: Trey Smack #28 of the Green Bay Packers celebrate a field goal against the Denver Broncos in the first half of the preseason game at Empower Field At Mile High on August 21, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Jamie Schwaberow/Getty Images) | Getty Images For a second straight preseason game, the Green Bay Packers got a magnificent performance out of rookie kicker Trey Smack. In the Packers’ 33-13 win over the Denver Broncos on Friday night, Smack had another perfect night, hitting all four of his field goal attempts. Similarly to his debut in Pittsburgh, Smack also booted a pair of those attempts from 50-plus yards, this time hitting from 51 and 59 in the thin Denver air. He also was perfect on three extra points as well, and he still has yet to miss a kick in preseason game action. It’s a big second data point for Smack, and these early returns are great for the team, which traded up to select Smack in the 6th round of the 2026 NFL Draft. Earlier this week, we asked Acme Packing Company readers about how confident they were that Smack would solve the team’s recent kicking woes. The results of that survey are below, but in summary, Packers fans felt great after Smack’s first preseason game: More than 70 percent of survey respondents said that they were either “somewhat” or “very” confident in Smack, with only six percent in an “uncertain” category. (21 percent were neutral or had no opinion.) After Friday’s performance, that confidence rating would surely increase even further. None of Smack’s kicks have yet come with a game on the line, so his clutch abilities still have yet to be put to the test. However, if he can deliver late in games the way he has so far in the preseason, the Packers should have an excellent opportunity to exceed the 9.5 win total set for the team by FanDuel and other sportsbooks.

title: Packers Depth Chart: Who played for Green Bay’s 1s and 2s vs. the Broncos?
summary: If you’re new here, we track who plays with the first- and second-team offensive and defensive units for the Green Bay Packers throughout the preseason because it’s a much cleaner picture of what the team looks like than the overall snap count. When third-stringers are in the game in the first half, like they were […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - AUGUST 16: Green Bay Packers Cornerback Kamal Hadden (36) warms up for the NFL preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and the Indianapolis Colts on August 16, 2025, at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If you’re new here, we track who plays with the first- and second-team offensive and defensive units for the Green Bay Packers throughout the preseason because it’s a much cleaner picture of what the team looks like than the overall snap count. When third-stringers are in the game in the first half, like they were on Friday against the Denver Broncos, things get muddied up a lot more than a regular-season game, where any playing time means a player is being made a priority. Last week, we broke down what the depth chart looked like against the Pittsburgh Steelers . Today, we’re going to compare and contrast what some of the differences are — if there were any — at each position. At the end of the article, after showing our work with the first- and second-team units, we’re going to drop a full depth chart of every position on the team. I hope you enjoy the content. Packers 1st Team Offense Quarterback Jordan Love: 12 snaps Like last week, Jordan Love got one drive in the game. For what it’s worth, head coach Matt LaFleur said that the plan is to play the starters in the team’s joint practice against the Arizona Cardinals (coached by his little brother), and to rest the starters in the final preseason game of 2026. Running Back MarShawn Lloyd: 8 snaps Chris Brooks: 4 snaps With Josh Jacobs (groin) out, MarShawn Lloyd remained the top ball-carrier with the first-team unit. Last week, Lloyd took all nine snaps, while he split a few reps with Chris Brooks, who was inactive last week with a hamstring injury, this time around. Receiver Matthew Golden: 9 snaps Christian Watson: 9 snaps Bo Melton: 4 snaps Skyy Moore: 3 snaps Savion Williams: 2 snaps For the most part, Skyy Moore took up the snaps that Jayden Reed (out with an ankle) would have played this week. To make it simple, it really does seem like the team is treating Moore as Reed’s backup (the slot position), Bo Melton as Matthew Golden’s backup (the X position) and Savion Williams as Christian Watson’s backup (the Z position). That’s all you really need to know here. Tight End Josh Whyle: 12 snaps Drake Dabney: 9 snaps Yes, the Packers played 75 percent of their first-team snaps out of 12 (two-tight end) personnel against Denver. They ran a lot of outside zone and bootlegs on base downs, looking like the early version of the LaFleur offense when he was just a full season removed from being the offensive coordinator for the Los Angeles Rams. Maybe that’s why they’re looking for different bodies/types of players at guard compared to 2025, when they were more of a vertical running game? For what it’s worth, Josh Whyle has played 20 total snaps with the first-team offense through two games, while Drake Dabney has played 12. Whyle and Dabney have moved up the depth chart with Tucker Kraft still getting his feet wet after his ACL tear and Luke Musgrave being on the PUP list with a neck injury. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 12 snaps (LT) Jager Burton: 12 snaps (LG) Sean Rhyan: 12 snaps (C) Jacob Monk: 12 snaps (RG) Anthony Belton: 12 snaps (RT) This is the same lineup the Packers used to open up against the Steelers, as left guard Aaron Banks (knee) and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele (knee) continue to be held out when the bullets are live. Packers 2nd Team Offense Quarterback Tyrod Taylor: 21 snaps While some might want Kyle McCord to take over as the backup quarterback, it remained the Taylor Show on Friday. He’s taken all 34 snaps with the second-team offense, even if he only has eight completions and 38 yards to show for it. Running Back Chris Brooks: 9 snaps MarShawn Lloyd: 7 snaps Pierre Strong Jr.: 5 snaps MarShawn Lloyd played a couple of early snaps with the second-team offense, like he did last week, before handing it off to the rest of the backs. With Brooks now healthy, he played the most out of the Packers’ top healthy trio. Jaden Nixon, who got three snaps with the second-team offense, received none this week as Brook entered the lineup. Receiver Bo Melton: 18 snaps Isaiah Neyor: 15 snaps Skyy Moore: 8 snaps J. Michael Sturdivant: 7 snaps Will Sheppard: 4 snaps Here’s something interesting: Savion Williams didn’t play with the second-team offense at all. No injury has been reported for him, either. As of now, the team treating him like a starter and sitting him after the first-team unit got shut down is a possibility. Notably, he also didn’t return kicks to start the game — a role he previously played in Week 1. I wouldn’t make too much of Moore receiving fewer snaps than Isaiah Neyor, who stepped in for Williams with the second-teamers today. Moore has been a slot-exclusive player, like Reed, so his playing time is dependent on there not being a second tight end or running back on the field. Last week, when Williams was in the lineup with the 2s, Bo Melton and Williams played 11 snaps each, Moore played 9 in the slot and Neyor played 4 off the bench. It’s nice that J. Michael Sturdivant, who might have left the Broncos game with a concussion, and Will Sheppard were able to get a couple snaps with the second-team offense in this game. Tight End Drake Dabney: 19 snaps Messiah Swinson: 13 snaps So far, Dabney has played 30 snaps with the second-team offense and Messiah Swinson has played 18. These are the team’s fourth and fifth tight ends, when everyone is healthy. The problem: Two guys ahead of them aren’t healthy yet. Offensive Line John Williams: 21 snaps (LT) Jager Burton: 21 snaps (LG) Jacob Monk: 21 snaps (C) Donovan Jennings: 21 snaps (RG) Anthony Belton: 21 snaps (RT) Unlike last week, Jordan Morgan didn’t play snaps as the left tackle with the second-string unit, which pushed John Williams into the lineup. Otherwise, these are the same players who played with Tyrod Taylor under center against the Steelers. Packers 1st Team Defense Defensive Line Karl Brooks: 8 snaps Nazir Stackhouse: 6 snaps Chris McClellan: 6 snaps Jonathan Ford: 4 snaps Devonte Wyatt: 4 snaps Jaden Crumedy: 4 snaps Anthony Campbell: 3 snaps Alright, this one gets weird. The Packers used a starting defensive line of Devonte Wyatt and Karl Brooks on the ends and Jonathan Ford at nose tackle to start the game, but didn’t use Wyatt after the first drive. They also hardly used Brooks (who was sat with the rest of the starters on the first-team defense) on the first-team defense’s second drive versus Denver. Don’t make too much of this pecking order. Clearly, Nazir Stackhouse, Chris McClellan, Jonathan Ford, Anthony Campbell and Jaden Crumedy are all fighting for playing time. Interestingly, Warren Brinson didn’t play a single snap in this game, despite not being listed as a scratch by the Packers, unlike the other players who didn’t see action. This is also your reminder that Javon Hargrave is still missing preseason games, but returned to practice as he recovers from a knee injury. Edge Defender Lukas Van Ness: 10 snaps Barryn Sorrell: 8 snaps Brenton Cox Jr.: 5 snaps Collin Oliver: 2 snaps Nothing is shocking here. This seems to be the pecking order, at least while Micah Parsons (PUP, knee) and Dani Dennis-Sutton (illness) aren’t involved. For what it’s worth, Collin Oliver usually comes on the field on obvious passing situations, but otherwise this is a pretty clear 1-2-3-4 from the team. Off-Ball Linebacker Zaire Franklin: 14 snaps Edgerrin Cooper: 14 snaps These are your starting linebackers. Cornerback Keisean Nixon: 14 snaps Benjamin St-Juste: 8 snaps Brandon Cisse: 6 snaps Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse were the starters tonight, but Cisse dropped out with an injury right before the second defensive drive of the game. After the game, Cisse called the injury “ nothing serious .” Benjamin…
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: The Day After The Day After: The Houston Texans’ 22-20 preseason loss to the Las Vegas Raiders
summary: The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, some thoughts about Week 2 of the preseason: Another Reminder About Perspective: What transpires in preseason games, in most cases, […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 20: Dylan Laube #23 of the Las Vegas Raiders runs into the end zone for a touchdown during the third quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, some thoughts about Week 2 of the preseason: Another Reminder About Perspective: What transpires in preseason games, in most cases, has little to no bearing on what will transpire in the regular season. That is the accepted truism about the preseason. For the Texans, they hope that is the case. Blowing a 17-0 lead and seeing the Raiders go on a 19-0 run in the second half is not fun, even in the preseason. Much of that comeback came against 3rd/4th/5th stringers, but many of those players will be the back-end depth that all rosters require. One could argue that this result should make cut down day real easy, especially for the defenders that couldn’t get the Raiders off the field. However, how many big preseason “wins” did the Texans of the pre-Ryans days have only to see the regular season devolve into pain and misery? No fan ever enjoys a loss, but at least this should not matter much. The Right Side of the Texans Starting Oline: For this game, the Texans mixed up their starting 5 for the Oline. Rutledge started, but this time at LG with Neal Brown at center. Yet, it was Trent Brown at RT and Ed Ingram at RG that drove much of Houston’s success on the opening drive. Woody Marks gained all 37 of his rushing yards going behind those two. One drive does not an offense make but expect many a running play to go to the right when the season gets started. 2nd Half Short-Yardage Plays: This has been a rather unfortunate trend of the squad when short-yardage plays that are the NFL equivalent of “gimmie-puts” are far from that. Even on the opening drive, on a 2nd and 1, Houston attempted a Woody Marks run over the left side which went nowhere. At least Houston made up for it on the next play. Later, Houston faced two 3rd and 1s in the second quarter, converting both. Yet, the second half saw Houston face four plays where they needed 1 to 2 yards to get a first down. They failed all four times: 3rd Quarter: 2nd and 2: No gain 3rd and 2: Sack 4th Quarter: 2nd and 1: No gain 3rd and 1: -1 yard run. Again, perspective on players on the field, but that goes a long way to explaining why a) most of those players were playing the second half of a preseason game and b) Houston is 0-2 in the preseason. Brett Rypien and So Little Time: The life of a fringe NFL player is far from easy. Always waiting by the phone, getting little to no notice about where the next paycheck is coming from, and having very little time to get up to speed, especially if you get pressed into immediate playing time. So it was with Rypien. Sure, he’s been around in the NFL (11th team in 7 years) and he is familiar with Caley’s offense. However, having less than a week to get up to speed with an offense before getting thrown into significant game time is not exactly a formula for success. The second half of the game bore that out. Only 2 first downs in the entirety of the half for Houston, along with multiple communication issues. It is not all on Rypien, but for those fringe players that are fighting for their NFL lives, that did not help. No one budgets for injuries, and Houston had greater needs than QB3, but perhaps having that 4th arm before the preseason games began, so at least someone had more than a couple of practices under their belt, might have helped. Ex-Texans Playing on the Raiders: More than a few familiar faces were in Raiders’ Silver and Black. RB/Special Teams legend Dare Ogunbowale chipped in with 35 yards rushing and a TD; DL Thomas Booker logged a sack and 2 TFLs; DT Folorunso Fatukasi got into the act with 3 tackles (1 solo). WR Noah Brown even got into the action with an 11-yard reception for a 1st down. Whether they all make the final Raiders’ roster is up for debate, but they at least got some semblance of revenge on Houston. Fun with Numbers: 17: Largest Blown Lead in a Preseason Loss: How very Houston to blow a multi-score lead, even in the preseason. Thursday night reflected the Texans’ largest blown lead in preseason history. The previous record was 14 points, which the Texans “accomplished” twice: Against Tampa Bay in 2007 (Led 14-0, lost 31-24) and against New Orleans in 2012 (Led 14-0, lost 34-27). 2019: The Last Time the Texans Finished the Preseason with a Losing Record: Thursday’s loss also clinched a losing preseason for Houston. The 2019 squad went 1-3 in the preseason (Did manage to go 10-6 to win the AFC South). Since the resumption of the preseason in 2021 (no preseason in 2020), Houston clinched winning preseason records, going 12-4. Make it 12-6 now. GAME BALLS LB Wade Woodaz: There’s significant competition for that LB3 spot behind Al-Shaair and To’oTo’o. Woodaz used this national showcase to present his argument for that slot. His 80-yard Pick Six was about as emphatic a statement as a 4th round rookie could make, especially as he was among the starters for the defense on their opening drive. It wasn’t all perfect, as he only had 2 total tackles and took a bad angle that gave Raiders’ RB Dylan Laube a wide-open TD run in the 3rd quarter. After the game, it transpired that Woodaz injured his thumb but not expected to miss that much time. Still, for making the biggest play of Houston’s preseason to date, he gets a TDATDA game ball. TE Marlin Klein: Leading Texans receiver for the second straight game. Preseason stars should be taken with healthy caveats, but if he can emerge as a solid TE, potentially being the other part of the 12 formations that Caley holds dear and playing as well as he has these past two games, that can only be a good thing for the Texans. P Kai Kroeger: Given that the Texans cut Jake Stonehouse before the start of the preseason games, Kroeger had no extra pressure to play well. This game, Kroeger was on point. 4 of his 6 punts landed inside the two, including a Lob Wedge beauty that pinned the Raiders inside their 4-yard. He averaged over 48 yards a punt, and the Raiders only managed 5.0 yards/return on three tries. Do that in the regular season, and Houston will have few worries about the punting game. SHOULD BE FORCED TO GET MATCHING HAIR STYLES WITH LAS VEGAS RAIDERS’ OWNER MARK DAVIS PK Ka’imi Fairbairn (Kickoffs): The placekicking was good (2-2 on 50+ yard FGs, 2-2 on XPs). Kickoffs need some work. In the first half, Fairbairn needlessly kicked into the end-zone for touchback, giving the Raiders the ball at the 35. Then, on a subsequent kickoff he shanked it short of the landing zone, giving the Raiders the ball at the 40. The first half Raiders didn’t take too much advantage of those plays, but Fairbairn will need to get back into kickoff rhythm by the time the games start counting for real. Raiders Special Teams: 2 missed PATs, 4 penalties on punts. Their special teams unit is not going to have a fun day in the film session. With that, the home slate for Houston’s preseason comes to an end. They close out the last preseason game next Friday, August 28, at the Carolina Panthers. Kickoff slated for 6 p.m. CDT on your ABC affiliate.
author: l4blitzer

title: Colts backups get dominated at home by Falcons: Takeaways from Preseason Week 2
summary: Look, it’s only preseason, and it was a battle of backups, but I don’t necessarily know that I expected the Indianapolis Colts to get blown out at home to the tune of 34-6 to the Atlanta Falcons, after arguably getting the better of their visitor at Grand Park through two joint training camp practices earlier […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - AUGUST 22: Indianapolis Colts quarterback Riley Leonard (15) rolls out to throw a pass over Atlanta Falcons linebacker JD Bertrand (40) during the first quarter of play during a pre season game between the Atlanta Falcons and the Indianapolis Colts on August 22, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Look, it’s only preseason, and it was a battle of backups, but I don’t necessarily know that I expected the Indianapolis Colts to get blown out at home to the tune of 34-6 to the Atlanta Falcons, after arguably getting the better of their visitor at Grand Park through two joint training camp practices earlier in the week. This was an ugly one to watch, let alone attend, so we’ll try to do as many takeaways as we can stomach: Offense: Quarterback: If he wanted to stay in the QB2 race, 2nd-year quarterback Riley Leonard needed a rebound outing after a sluggish performance in his 2026 preseason debut last Thursday night, relieving Anthony Richardson Sr. in the second half of that game versus the New England Patriots, Instead, Leonard was just as bad, if not worse on Saturday afternoon against Atlanta. He completed 7 of 14 pass attempts for 62 passing yards (4.4 avg.), 0 touchdowns, 0 interceptions, and a fumble that was recovered. While he played well in the 2025 regular season finale against the Houston Texans first-team defense for a half, I’ve been stating throughout this offseason that it was a very limited sample size, while also acknowledging that Colts head coach Shane Steichen is a notoriously adept game scripter, especially in the first half of games. Right now, Leonard looks more the part of a developmental QB3, and the reason why Indianapolis elected to bring grizzled veteran Philip Rivers back 5 years removed from retirement, rather than throw Leonard to the wolves for last season’s final stretch of games. Richardson Sr. wasn’t particularly sharp in this one either, playing behind Indy’s offensive line of 3s, completing 3 of 9 pass attempts for 24 passing yards, but he looks to be the better bet to be the Colts QB2 right now. He at least has greater mobility in his favor. Running Back: Rookie 7th round pick Seth McGowan looks like he’s won the primary backup running back job behind star workhorse Jonathan Taylor. His final line wasn’t great in this one (8 carries for 27 total rushing yards), but he again had some good rushes . Fellow backup running back DJ Giddens wasn’t available in this one with a lingering hamstring injury, so the main backup job appears to be McGowan’s to lose right now. It’ll be interesting to see what the Colts plan on doing with Giddens, who was their 5th round pick from the 2025 NFL Draft, but endured some definite growing pains as a rookie. Wide Receiver: The rookie 7th round pick Deion Burks was another bright spot for the Colts, despite a quiet line of 4 receptions for 19 total receiving yards. He had a couple of nice catches in this one , and for a young wideout who could be on the roster bubble, made a stronger case to stick on the active 53-man roster. Helping Burks’ cause is that he was the Colts primary kick returner in this one and fared pretty well, as special teams versatility will definitely play for the bottom of Indy’s active roster players. Defense: Backup Cornerbacks: Backup Cam Taylor-Britt looked like he held his own and would realistically be the ’Next Man Up’ (*outside of his Week 1 suspension) if any of Indy’s top three cornerbacks miss time, but both fellow backup corners Mekhi Blackmon and Jonathan Edwards struggled for a consecutive preseason game. Each’s job security could be in jeopardy. If there was one thing to note, it’s that definite bubble cornerback Jaylon Jones actually played pretty well late in this one . Rotational Edges: 2025 2nd round pick Jaylahn Tuimoloau has yet to stand out at all running against the 2’s, and if there’s something to celebrate from their edge room (for a defense that had just one sack collectively on Saturday afternoon), rookie 5th round pick George Gumbs Jr. flashed again for a consecutive preseason game . He could be pushing for a larger rotational role, especially if Tuimoloau continues to be ‘just a guy’ out there from a pass rushing perspective. Rookie Linebackers: The rookie linebacker pairing of CJ Allen (3 tackles) and Bryce Boettcher (4 tackles) flashed their instincts in this one , and both should eventually contribute to the first-team defense in their first year—even in subpackage work, so this was good game day experience for them. Special Teams: Kickers: Blake Grupe has been consistently the stronger leg throughout training camp, but when the game day lights have come on through two preseason games, it’s actually been Spencer Shrader, who has been the stronger performer. Shrader converted his two field goals kicks: 48 and 53 yards , while Grupe’s 36-yard field goal attempt was wide right. Grupe appeared to be in the driver’s seat ahead of preseason, but now, it’s a fair question of whether Shrader, who has performed well during actual game days (albeit preseason) carries more weight right now than Grupe being close to automatic kicking in practice, with less pressure.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts depth gets exposed in preseason blowout loss to Falcons
summary: INDIANAPOLIS — There was nowhere to hide, especially not behind the home faithful inside Lucas Oil Stadium. Not even behind the preseason label, because the game itself exposed a bit more. The depth of the Indianapolis Colts was tested in Saturday’s preseason home opener as the Atlanta Falcons dominated with an overwhelming score of 34-6. […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts kicker Spencer Shrader makes a 48-yard field goal in the final practice session of Thursday’s joint-practice with the Atlanta Falcons at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, Ind. — Aug. 20, 2026. | Thomas Butler-Guerrero INDIANAPOLIS — There was nowhere to hide, especially not behind the home faithful inside Lucas Oil Stadium. Not even behind the preseason label, because the game itself exposed a bit more. The depth of the Indianapolis Colts was tested in Saturday’s preseason home opener as the Atlanta Falcons dominated with an overwhelming score of 34-6. It wasn’t just that the Falcons piled up points on four of their five drives in the first half, or that they needed just four plays to march into the end zone to start the second half. For Indianapolis, the numbers were ugly from virtually every angle. The Colts were forced to punt seven times, committed eight penalties, started 0-for-9 on third down and collected only 91 total yards of offense with their second unit. Second-year quarterback Riley Leonard got the start on Saturday to command the second-team offense, but finished 7-of-14 passing for just 62 yards in the first half. Three of those seven completions came essentially in garbage time, when the Colts had no realistic chance of moving the ball into scoring range with the personnel on the field to end of the first half. Indianapolis’ first five possessions lasted just 24 plays and gained a total of 70 yards. The Colts finally crossed midfield late in the first quarter after a defensive pass interference penalty against the Falcons was followed by an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty, which gifted them 31 extra yards. Kicker Spencer Shrader salvaged a pair of first quarter possessions by making a 48-yard field goal and a 53-yarder, but that was as much as the Colts could muster on the scoreboard. The lone true offensive highlight of the game was when Leonard found slot receiver Coleman Owen wide open for a 39-yard gain. Indianapolis used a trips formation with Owen motioning into the mix before running a scissors concept that left him uncovered on a corner route to march into Falcons territory. Big completion to Coleman Owen. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/YF66Jhtz9F — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 Atlanta repeatedly found ways to attack Indianapolis’ secondary, particularly cornerback Mekhi Blackmon, who was flagged for pass interference twice during a 12-play drive. Atlanta eventually faced fourth-and-3 from the Colts’ 6-yard line, but another pass interference call against Blackmon kept the drive alive and gave the Falcons first-and-goal at the 1-yard-line. Three plays later, Nick Carter powered in for a 1-yard touchdown, taking a big hit from linebacker Austin Ajiake before spinning his way onto the goal line. With less than a minute left before halftime, Falcons quarterback Jack Strand rolled into play-action and found running back Cash Jones wide open in the flat for a 13-yard touchdown. No Colts defender had a realistic chance to make a play before Jones was about to cross the goal line. Suddenly, the Colts were staring at an 18-point deficit heading into halftime and it only got worse from there. Atlanta needed just four plays to reach the end zone on their opening possession of the second half. After Strand launched a 36-yard completion down the right sideline to breach the red zone, he tucked it himself and scampered 16 yards for a rushing touchdown to extend the lead to 31-6 less than two minutes into the half. The only audible cheers roared when quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr. entered to take over with the third stringers, but even his athleticism couldn’t spark Indianapolis’ offense. His first possession began with a 17-yard completion to receiver Raylen Sharpe that was nullified by an offensive pass interference penalty on Pharaoh Brown, which of course, forced another punt three plays later. Richardson’s second drive began backed up at Indy’s own 3-yard line as he was tasked to lead an offense of third-stringers nearly the entire length of the field. It predictably went nowhere as Richardson nearly threw an interception while trying to escape pressure in his own end zone, then he was stuffed at the line of scrimmage on the next snap. By the start of the fourth quarter, the Colts had punted six times, while picking up just four first downs. Richardson completed just 3-of-9 passes for a mere 24 passing yards and added 15 rushing yards on three carries. Even when they finally earned their fifth first down, an inside run by running back Anderson Castle that gained 10 yards, the drive ultimately went backward. The disorganization continued as a dropped pass by Sahmir Hagans was followed by a false start, then a sack on third down terminated the possession and forced Indianapolis to punt again. Despite moving the sticks, the Colts’ ninth drive finished with a net loss of two yards. The scoreboard ultimately means nothing in the grand scheme, but the performance in the preseason home opener exposed something Indianapolis cannot ignore. Depth matters over the course of a season. When the Colts caught the injury bug last season, it flipped the campaign upside down. After an NFL-best 8-2 start, the Colts lost their final seven games of the 2025 regular season to free fall out of the AFC playoff race. The Colts entered the second preseason game hoping to evaluate the players fighting for roster spots and establish which reserves could be trusted when injuries inevitably spring during the regular season. Instead, the backups were sloppy and inefficient. The offense struggled to sustain drives, while the defense spent nearly 39 minutes trying to stop the Falcons. Sure, Indianapolis could have been shut out, but that misses the point. For 60 minutes, the Colts produced one explosive passing play and one explosive run when the game was out of reach. Two of their first four first downs through the first three frames were granted because of Atlanta penalties. At home, the Colts reserves were completely exposed. With many roster decisions looming over the next week, Saturday’s performance should be a stark reminder that the difference between a competitive contender and one that can be overwhelmed by its opponent isn’t found just at the top of the depth chart. Against Atlanta, Indianapolis’ depth on both sides of the ball had nowhere to hide.
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: The Colts Go-To Preseason Play: Choice + Snag Basic
summary: Everyone remembers the infamous snap Anthony Richardson took to kickoff the QB competition in Baltimore. You know, the one that set Twitter on fire that night? It’s very rare that a preseason play would cause this much debate. After all, the preseason is as vanilla as it gets. But Anthony Richardson took a lot of […]
full_text: Everyone remembers the infamous snap Anthony Richardson took to kickoff the QB competition in Baltimore. You know, the one that set Twitter on fire that night? Anthony Richardson running it. pic.twitter.com/806Bewbrvz — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) August 17, 2026 It’s very rare that a preseason play would cause this much debate. After all, the preseason is as vanilla as it gets. But Anthony Richardson took a lot of heat, literally and figuratively, for not seeing the free runner and taking a massive shot in an exhibition game. Most people blamed Richardson’s lack of understanding of the protection, while others quietly wondered if this was a poor play design. Well, the Colts ran it again this year.. And this time it was an interception. This is a base play from the Colts. They run it at least once a preseason game. Choice + Snag Basic as a backside concept. Same play that AR got hurt on in Baltimore last year. Going to do a larger breakdown on this play for @StampedeBlue pic.twitter.com/nLVYGuPsL6 — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) August 17, 2026 Let’s breakdown the play further, and why potentially it’s given the Colts some trouble. WHAT HAPPENED WHEN RICHARDSON RAN IT IN BALTIMORE? There’s a lot of philosophies to handling pressure from a defense. You can try to block it up or you can invite the pressure and throw hot no matter what. The Colts historically have gone with the former. On the Baltimore play, the Ravens are running a very common pressure called Whip Fire Zone. The idea is to get the OL to slide one way, and bring an extra rusher from the weak side. So why was AR not looking at the free rusher? The Colts decided to slide to the side of the QB’s first read. There’s nothing illegal about this, but it sure makes it harder on the QB. The first read on this play is the choice route, so in order to be the most protected in the opposite direction in where the QB’s looking, you want to slide away from that side. As the Colts ran it in 2024, it’s on Anthony Richardson to know he’s hot in 5 man protection and throw to the back on the other side of the field, like many other QBs in other systems would. A variety of systems would handle this a variety of different ways. It was a blurry rep at best. WHAT HAPPENED IN NEW ENGLAND? The Colts pair this concept with a motion from the Z receiver to try and get a tell on the defense. The safety travels with the Z receiver motioning to the other side of the field. Before the ball is snapped it looks like weak rotated Cover 3. Whether this is a true pure progression read that always starts with the choice, or Richardson is working away from the perceived rotation pre-snap, he starts with the choice. Notice this time the Colts are sliding away from the choice. This makes me think it’s probably a pure progression read. The Patriots at the snap bail into a Cover 8 (Cover 2 to passing strength, Cover 4 away) look and the field corner is squatting on the choice route. It’s a really good rep from the Patriots defense. I don’t know if the Colts give the QB the option to the throw the hole shot, or they ask the QB to progress to the Snag side, but in my opinion, I’d like to see Richardson progress off the choice. Yes the ball needs to be caught, and it’s a fine throw, but also into quasi double coverage. BOTTOM LINE If nothing else, it’s absolutely fascinating that two of Anthony Richardson’s most controversial preseason plays came on the exact same concept. Given how we’ve seen the Colts re-design the play in 2026, it appears like the staff felt like in 2024 they should have slid away from the first read. It’s also possible that Anthony Richardson in year 3 has more autonomy to dictate the slides. Either way, I don’t think this is a call that Shane Steichen will go-to if Anthony Richardson sees in action in 2026.
author: coltsfilmroom

title: Preseason Week 2 Colts vs. Falcons Game Thread
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are at home to take on the Atlanta Falcons in week 2 of the 2026 preseason, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. Folks, the season is almost upon us but today we get to experience the greatness that is the preseason. This past week the Colts and Falcons had joint practices so we shouldn’t […]
full_text: The Indianapolis Colts are at home to take on the Atlanta Falcons in week 2 of the 2026 preseason, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. Folks, the season is almost upon us but today we get to experience the greatness that is the preseason. This past week the Colts and Falcons had joint practices so we shouldn’t expect to see much from the starters in this one but there will still be plenty to watch for. Today I’ll have an eye on the rookies. Second round pick CJ Allen will be suiting up for his first action of the preseason. Everyone expects Allen to have a big role this season so it will be good to see how he preforms today. Really excited to see what (we hope) the future of the linebacker position looks like for Indy. Caden Curry was all over the field last week against the Patriots and this week I hope he gets some burn earlier in the game to see if he can repeat his success. His short arms kept him from being drafted before the sixth round, but his motor and production from last week should have earned him a shot at a bigger role this week. Last week we saw AJ Halucy get some playing time early on. Halucy didn’t stand out a ton but he got in on several stops and for a young guy everyone hopes will have a big role this season. Halucy won’t suit up today, which is disappointing, but understandable. Bryce Boettcher was another guy that made a big impact a week ago and I’ll be interested to see if the former Oregon Duck can repeat his exciting performance. George Gumbs Jr. surprised me last week. In my eyes Gumbs was a developmental prospect, a guy that probably wouldn’t show much but had the physical tools to compete for a rotational role in a couple of years. And that might still be true but Gumbs ended week one with a sack and three tackles. All reports indicate he has looked good in camp, also. On offense the guy I’m most looking forward to seeing is guard Jalen Farmer. Farmer looked very good in week one, moving piles in the run game while holding up well in pass protection. I don’t know that he’ll beat out Matt Goncalves for week one but I do know that it’s been a long time since I felt this good about the team’s depth at guard. Seth McGowan sure looked better than most guys who are picked 237 overall a week ago. Part of that was due to a pretty serious off the field issue, but that notwithstanding, McGowan might already have locked down the RB2 role behind Jonathan Taylor and another strong showing should cement that. Fellow seventh rounder Deion Burks is in a battle for a roster spot. If he can show more on offense that would be great but he really needs to stand out on special teams this week to give the team a reason to bet on him once roster cut downs arrive. And like everyone else I’ll be paying attention to the QB2 battle. A week ago Riley Leonard was not good while Anthony Richardson started rough and ended well. Leonard should get most of the snaps early in this one so it will be interesting to see how he does playing with more guys who will make the roster. That said, I don’t have high hopes. I will be watching the Falcons side of the aisle for former Colts running back Tyler Goodson. It seems like Goodson has secured the RB3 role in Atlanta and I’m happy for him. Goodson seemed like a good guy and was a solid back during his time in Indy. I’m also hoping he gets to enjoy a nice winter in the South as I’m already dreading what’s coming for us in the Midwest. Week two of the preseason is about the time people start complaining that the games aren’t good and they just want the regular season to be here and I get it. But man, I’m just happy football is back in any form. Prediction: Falcons: 23 Colts: 23 As always, go Colts. RELATED What to Watch For with Luke Schultheis This is your preseason week two open thread so hang out here, chat, celebrate, commiserate, and argue in the comments! Go wild (within reason)! Go Colts!

title: What to Watch For: Colts host Falcons for Preseason Week 2
summary: The Indianapolis Colts (0-0-1) host the Atlanta Falcons (0-1) for their home preseason opener at Saturday afternoon at 1 PM EST on CBS4, and the Horseshoe Faithful can listen in at 93.5 and 107.5 The Fan. Matt Taylor (play-by-play) and Charles Arbuckle (analyst) will be on the radio call, with former longtime coach Rick Venturi […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 20: Indianapolis Colts linebacker Austin Ajiake (58) runs past Atlanta Falcons running back Tyler Goodson (25) during the Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons joint training camp practice on August 20, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (0-0-1) host the Atlanta Falcons (0-1) for their home preseason opener at Saturday afternoon at 1 PM EST on CBS4, and the Horseshoe Faithful can listen in at 93.5 and 107.5 The Fan. Matt Taylor (play-by-play) and Charles Arbuckle (analyst) will be on the radio call, with former longtime coach Rick Venturi moving into the TV booth as an analyst for this preseason. For the Colts, starters are not expected to play again. Meanwhile, backup quarterback Riley Leonard will get the start for the first half, with Anthony Richardson Sr. coming in relief of him to start the second half. Similarly to Indianapolis, Atlanta is also not expected to play its starters. Quarterbacks Jack Strand and Cooper Rush are expected to split the positional workload for the Falcons. Things that I’ll be Watching For: Backup Running Spot: Rookie Seth McGowan has seemingly surpassed 2nd-year rusher DJ Giddens, who’s been battling a hamstring issue during training camp recently, behind star workhorse Jonathan Taylor. Giddens just returned to practice later this week, but does he have enough time to hold off Ulysses Bentley IV for the 3rd running back spot at this point? Rookie right guard Jalen Farmer flashed in his preseason debut and looks like the Colts top swing-tackle option, should they need an extra offensive lineman this season. Veteran Laquon Treadwell’s continued future with the Colts could be in question after the signing of fellow veteran Keenan Allen. With Ashton Dulin potentially being bumped down back to special teams gunner work, would Indianapolis prefer to keep rookie 7th round pick Deion Burks over the regarded veteran Treadwell? Special teams versatility could play a factor there, as Treadwell remains very good there. The rotational backup edge group of Jaylahn Tuimoloau, George Gumbs Jr., and Caden Curry. Tuimoloau was stifled against 2’s, while the pair of rookies, Gumbs Jr. and Curry, flashed against lesser competition. Offensive line depth in the NFL gets pretty rough once you get past the second teams, but at a certain point, Tuimoloau has to start consistently making an impact if he wants to hold off the newcomers going forward. CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher as a rookie pairing at linebacker for the Colts. Both Jaylon Carlies and Akeem Davis-Gaither continued to run with the first-team defense in training camp late, which means Allen and Boettcher should be in line to get the start with the 2nd-team defense in this one. Their instincts, speed, and athleticism should be fun to watch out there. They should still see subpackage work as rookies. Cornerbacks behind the starters. Both Mekhi Blackmon and Jonathan Edwards had rough showings in coverage last week. It was Week 1 of preseason, but with veteran Charvarius Ward’s injury history, the Colts need a capable ‘Next Man Up’. Maybe that guy is Cam Taylor-Britt, but both Blackmon and Edwards need to show more than they did last Thursday night. Additionally, how long former starter Jaylon Jones plays into the second half in this one could be a forewarning toward his continued Colts job security. The ongoing Colts kicking battle. Spencer Shrader at least slightly redeemed himself in Preseason Week 1 after his training camp kicking struggles, especially in comparison to his kicking counterpart Blake Grupe, who had largely been automatic. To me, Grupe still holds a slight edge, but if Shrader has another strong showing when the bright lights actually come on (I know it’s still preseason!), maybe that’s the difference.
