full_text: Jan 18, 2025; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels (5) looks to pass defended by Detroit Lions defensive back Brian Branch (32) during the second half at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: David Reginek-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Daily Slop – 22 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Anybody remember the last time the Commanders went to Detroit?! What a night pic.twitter.com/wRrHbugSd8 — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) August 21, 2026 Articles Commanders.com Mailbag: Soft tissue injuries & kick returners How comfortable is the staff that Trey Amos will be ready to go for Week 1 in Philly? He’s practiced once since November 2025. It seems like Amos is making good progress with his ankle, so hopefully he will be on the field soon and get a few more practices under him before Week 1. But your question is a fair one, because that’s a long time between games. I don’t know how the Commanders will handle his ramp-up process if it goes into the season, but if it’s anything like how they handled Brandon Coleman’s recovery process two years ago, they aren’t just going to throw him into the starting lineup. That wouldn’t be fair to anyone. They’ll likely ease him into things, giving him a handful of plays that will increase each week. Fortunately, the Commanders have players like Rasul Douglas and Amik Robertson who have looked impressive in camp, so the Commanders can afford to take their time with Amos. Why is DQ taking precautions for soft tissue injuries? This is football and how are we supposed to build chemistry when we go a week of practice and the 1s aren’t playing together Because soft tissue injuries are tricky, and if you’re not careful, they can become much worse. I didn’t think I would have to put on my medical hat for this, but here we go. Soft tissue areas, like hamstrings, get a limited amount of blood flow compared to bones. They’re also required for us to move, which makes it harder for them to heal. They can be some of the most tedious injuries to heal from because the recovery process involves significantly limiting movement and slowly ramping things up to get the tissue back up to full strength. (I think it’s also appropriate to mention that I’m not a doctor or physical therapist. This is solely based on my personal experience with soft tissue injuries, so please don’t take my word as gospel.) But here’s the real reason why Dan Quinn and other teams take soft tissue injuries seriously and have a cautious approach with rehabbing players who deal with them: a completely torn hamstring can take, at most, six months to heal, meaning that player would miss the entire season. That, of course, is just not ideal, so to avoid that, you have to be cautious with them, because strains are when they are the most vulnerable. I can empathize with fans getting frustrated with players getting injured. I also want this team to be at full strength all the time, because I have high expectations for this season. But I also know the players and coaches are more frustrated. They want to play and give themselves the best chance to win, but it’s also their livelihood. Plus, I promise you that Dan Quinn would much rather have his players on the field instead of in the training room. Who are the team’s kick returners? I think they are still trying to figure that out. McCaffrey had some productive returns before his injury. He’s more of a straight-line runner, but he knows how to follow his blockers. He’s listed as the starting kick returner on the unofficial depth chart, so take that for what you will. With that said, I think players like Henry are making the case to be the second kick returner. Henry’s quickness would be an asset on special teams, and it will play a vital role in whether he can make the roster. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Commanders vs Lions Preview: 3 story lines to watch Sonny Styles’ Second Start Say that five times fast. The centerpiece of Washington’s re-tooled defense delivered a solid—if quiet—first series in his NFL debut. But it was just one series. It is unfair to label a 21-year-old rookie “tentative” based on 14 snaps, especially considering he was immediately handed green-dot play-calling duties to align his teammates. Styles flashed his high-end athletic traits against Miami, showing impressive range and depth in pass coverage. This week, I want to see him play fast from the opening whistle and trigger aggressively on his run fits. What to Watch: Can the rookie play fast and shoot gaps to make plays at or behind the line of scrimmage? Furthermore, will fellow linebacker Leo Chenal step up? The high-priority free agent has had a relatively quiet camp so far. He was brought in to be a stout run defender, but we have yet to see him fully unleash that style in game action. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Yard Barker Terry McLaurin compares himself to Stefon Diggs During an appearance on the Commanders’ “Next Man Up,” McLaurin offered a colorful description of his early relationship with Diggs. The similarities apparently became obvious once the two receivers started working together. “I kind of think of that Spider-Man meme where they’re both pointing at each other,” McLaurin said. “We’re the same guy on the field.” McLaurin explained that both receivers bring passion, leadership and considerable energy to the offense. Neither player has built a career by quietly blending into the background. Diggs has earned four Pro Bowl selections and one first-team All-Pro honor during his career. McLaurin has made the Pro Bowl twice while consistently producing despite Washington’s revolving door at quarterback. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Meet the NFL’s top players 25 and under. Coaches, scouts, execs rank them heading into 2026 Jayden Daniels, QB, Washington Commanders. Age: 25 (12/18/00) Daniels turned Washington into a contender during a rookie season that saw him post a completion percentage of 69.0, the highest by a first-year quarterback in NFL history. His mobility makes him a constant threat. The Commanders just need to keep him healthy. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illlustrated 5 Biggest Questions Still Unanswered Entering Commanders Preseason Week 2 Who Is Actually Winning the Center Job? The center position has become more than a question mark at this point after projected starter Nick Allegretti missed most of camp ; Julian Good-Jones absorbed the majority of that load, while rookie Matt Gulbin continues to make his own push. The problem is, Good-Jones didn’t look very, well, good in the first preseason game against Miami. That doesn’t change how the staff views him, but it certainly suggests they aren’t comfortable with him as the center. Allegretti returned to practice this week, but before that session ended, he had what Quinn called “a light setback,” which causes even more delays in getting Jayden Daniels ready for the season, as the two must build some sort of chemistry. Allegretti’s injury opened the door for Quinn to notice the guys behind him. “Both guys are really starting to make a move,” Quinn said, with Gulbin coming off a clean preseason opener and Good-Jones having accumulated significant work since early in camp. “So, over the next two weeks, or maybe two and a half weeks, we’ll call it,” he said. “I’d like to see what that rotation looks like with the three of these guys.” The Real Question : Can Gulbin or Good-Jones create actual separation while Allegretti’s availability remains inconsistent? title: Would you cut electric Robert Henry or physical Kaytron Allen?
summary: The hardest decisions belong to the best rosters A deep roster complicates the final roster cutdown to 53 players. In the early stages of a franchise rebuild, roster cuts are straightforward because the talent drop-off past the top 35 players is steep. However, when depth increases across the board, NFL front offices are forced to […]
full_text: The h ardest decisions belong to the best rosters A deep roster complicates the final roster cutdown to 53 players. In the early stages of a franchise rebuild, roster cuts are straightforward because the talent drop-off past the top 35 players is steep. However, when depth increases across the board, NFL front offices are forced to expose genuinely talented players to waivers. This dilemma is evident in the offensive backfield of the 2026 Commanders. Historically, most NFL teams carry either three or four running backs on their initial 53-man roster, depending in part on special teams value. Under general manager Adam Peters and head coach Dan Quinn, the Washington Commanders have aligned with this standard. In 2024 , the Commanders kept four running backs on the initial roster. In 2025 , the team did the same, starting out with Austin Ekeler, Jeremy McNichols, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, and Chris Rodriguez Jr. However, when Ekeler was lost for the season in Week 2, he was not replaced on the roster and the team went through most of the season with just three running backs. Entering the final weeks of the 2026 preseason, locking onto a hard cap of four running backs would have a direct, cascading effect on the rest of the offense. If Washington keeps a fourth running back, they cannot expand depth at other positions. For instance, carrying an extra back means deciding whether to risk a developmental sixth or seventh wide receiver on waivers, or to squeeze the tight-end room down to a strict trio. In effect, the decision to keep a player at one position represents a sacrificed depth piece at another like quarterback, receiver, or tight end. The Commanders may want to keep three QBs, seven WRs, four TEs and four RBs, but the math simply won’t work out, and that means that some NFL-quality skill players are going to find themselves missing out on the Commanders 53-man roster in 2026. In this week’s Reacts survey, we asked Hogs Haven readers to focus on the running back position and decide, based on the information available to date, which of the team’s top four running backs would miss out if Adam Peters and Dan Quinn chose to keep only three on the initial roster. The Power of Pedigree: draft capital vs. the undrafted tag Roster battles are often talked about as if they take place in a strict meritocracy, but, in reality, draft pedigree heavily influences both front-office security and fan perception. Bill Croskey-Merritt enters 2026 with a year of NFL experience under his belt after being selected in the seventh round. Rookie Kaytron “Fatman” Allen carries the shield of a sixth-round draft choice. Rookie Robert Henry Jr. faces the steeper climb of an undrafted college free agent. The recent Hogs Haven poll, which asked readers to choose one back to leave off the roster, reflects this reality: Visit our partners at FanDuel Henry, the UDFA rookie , at 60%, is the popular choice to miss out on a 3-man running back room, while Allen, drafted in the sixth-round back in April, would be the choice of 26% of survey respondents. This disparity may highlight a clear psychological bias toward draft investment, or it may reflect the relative skills and play style of the members of the running back room. The first preseason game vs the Miami Dolphins Both rookies had excellent NFL debuts last Friday night in Landover : Kaytron Allen handled a heavy workload, rushing 23 times for 85 yards and a touchdown. It was a productive but grinding debut that averaged a modest 3.7 yards per carry. Robert Henry Jr. had 12 carries for 75 yards and a touchdown, and delivered the game’s signature play, exploding past the defense for a 22-yard rushing touchdown. Despite Henry having been the rookie back who generated the most excitement and greatest efficiency against Miami, it is he, Henry, and not Allen whom most survey respondents would leave off the roster. Draft pedigree Consider a hypothetical scenario where these two players’ draft pedigrees were perfectly reversed—Henry selected in the sixth round and Allen signed as an undrafted free agent. It feels like fan expectations entering the offseason and training camp might well have been reversed, and that the Reacts poll results might have been quite different based on last week’s preseason production against the Miami Dolphins. Had Henry carried the sixth-round label, his explosive touchdown run would likely have been heralded as proof of a draft-day steal, and his spot on the 53-man roster might well be considered secure. Conversely, if Allen were undrafted, his 23-carry workload could have been viewed as the team simply burning camp reps on a disposable asset, with his 3.7 yards per carry being seen as the unsurprising pedestrian output of an undrafted player. We know that fans and evaluators instinctively give drafted players a longer leash, viewing their struggles as temporary adjustment periods while assuming undrafted players have a lower absolute ceiling. The ‘style’ argument While draft status undoubtedly influences fan perception, a more strategic explanation for these poll results lies in rational understanding of structural roster construction and stylistic synergy. Knowledgeable fans, as we know, look beyond raw efficiency metrics to evaluate how a player’s skill set complements the existing depth chart. The Commanders backfield is anchored by Rachaad White and Bill Croskey-Merritt, both of whom excel as explosive, one-cut slashers tailored for outside-zone concepts. Henry Jr.’s dynamic 22-yard touchdown run showcased that exact same explosive, perimeter-oriented profile. Voting to keep Henry in a three-man running back room would give Washington a trio of outside runners, creating a highly redundant skill set in the position group. While explosive, this would leave a massive hole in the skill set of the position for Washington. “Fatman” Allen offers a distinctly different, complementary identity. Despite his lower yards-per-carry average against Miami, Allen’s physical, low-center-of-gravity style is built for running between the tackles and grinding out tough yards against stacked boxes – something that every NFL team needs. With the majority of Hogs Haven readers voting to keep Allen over Henry, they demonstrated a rational understanding of role optimization. They recognize that Allen provides the essential short-yardage and goal-line versatility that the roster would otherwise lack, making him a more logical puzzle piece for the final 53 than his redundant, albeit electric, counterpart. The Mason-Brennan paradox The survey results with respect to Robert Henry Jr. present a stark contrast – a paradox if you will — in fan sentiment. In a separate Hogs Haven survey exploring which young player generated the most “hype” following the Dolphins game, Henry dominated the field with 68% of the total vote. The contrast between these two surveys illustrates the difference between rewarding an exciting moment and constructing a viable 53-man roster. A 22-yard touchdown run is a highly visible, electric highlight that generates organic fan excitement. It provides immediate optimism for a fan base looking for hidden gems. However, when forced to make tough roster decisions, those same knowledgeable fans recognize the baseline floor required for the regular season. They understand that a complete NFL running back must reliably pass-protect, contribute on special teams, and sustain tough yardage down to down. While 68% of fans enjoy the flashes of talent Henry brings to the field, 60% logically conclude that Allen is the better fit for the Commanders running back room. If the Commanders keep four running backs on the initial roster, chances are high that both rookies make the team and contribute to the ’26 season. On the other hand, if the demands of roster construction constrain the number of running backs to just 3 to open the season, a tough choice will need to be made, and Hogs Haven readers see Allen as the right choice…

title: 2026 NFL preseason Week 2: Game takeaways, analysis
summary: NFL Nation reporters tackle the biggest looming roster questions coming off each NFL Week 2 preseason game.
full_text:
Week 2 of the  2026 NFL preseason kicked off Thursday, giving us more insight into position battles and the push to make 53-man rosters before the cut-down deadline Aug. 30. Action began with two games Thursday before Friday's three games, with severe weather rolling through Jacksonville late in the fourth quarter -- causing league and team officials to end the game because of lightning at the two-minute warning.

 Things continued Saturday with 10 games, including  Cleveland Browns QB Deshaun Watson 's first home game since tearing his right Achilles tendon in October 2024 and a game in which he was met with loud boos, and Minnesota Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy getting "banged up" during a rough first quarter in a loss to the Ravens.

 And Sunday's game wraps up the weekend with the  Seattle Seahawks at the  Tennessee Titans  ( 8 p.m. ET, Fox) .

 Our NFL Nation reporters picked out what you need to know about big roster decisions and more coming off Week 2 of the preseason.

 
 Quick links: 
 Full NFL schedule | Where to watch 
 Depth charts  | Sign up to play fantasy 

 

 

 Saturday's results 

 Cowboys 34, Cardinals 13 
 

 Cowboys: Has Joe Milton III separated himself in the No. 2 quarterback battle? Milton's command of the offense is so much greater than it was in 2025, and the results have been telling. In two games, he has completed 21 of 28 passes for 286 yards and three touchdowns. He also ran for a score. He has made the big plays -- a TD of 56 yards and a completion of 70 yards vs. the Cardinals -- but more importantly, he avoided mistakes.

 Milton's arm strength is unquestioned, but his poise and decision-making have impressed the coaches. Sam Howell has done nothing to lose the job (though that late-game pick with the Cowboys in the red zone against Arizona didn't help), but the roster gymnastics required by keeping three quarterbacks on the 53-man roster could be too costly when the Cowboys look to fill their spots at wide receiver, linebacker and cornerback. -- Todd Archer 

 Next game: vs New Orleans Saints (Thursday, 8 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited)

 

 Cardinals: What does the bottom of the wide receiver room look like? There are a few guarantees to make the roster: Marvin Harrison Jr ., Michael Wilson , Kendrick Bourne and Devin Duvernay . After that, there are two questions: How many receivers will Arizona keep and who will the rest of them be?

 There are essentially three options for the last two (possibly three) spots: Simi Fehoko , Reggie Virgil and Jalen Brooks . Brooks has played great this preseason, and Wilson called Fehoko one of the best preseason receivers of all time. He plays a big role on special teams, so that will factor in. Virgil is a rookie who's quick and has shown promise. If Arizona keeps six WRs, Brooks might be the odd man out but won't last long on the practice squad, and if Virgil gets cut, Brooks could last a little longer. -- Josh Weinfuss 

 Next game: at Green Bay Packers (Friday, 8 p.m. ET)

 
 Patriots 24, Eagles 21 
 

 Patriots: Did veteran cornerback Kindle Vildor play his way onto the roster? The Patriots' top three at the position are solidified --  Christian Gonzalez , Carlton Davis III and  Marcus Jones  -- and coaches seem committed to third-year player Charles Woods as the fourth option. Vildor (seventh year) would be competing for a fifth or possibly sixth spot, and he made a case with tight coverage and two pass breakups Saturday. He also had a would-be interception nullified by an unnecessary roughness penalty on OLB Gabe Jacas . Vildor (5-11, 190) had an INT in Week 1.

 Other questions of note: Did Lan Larison 's strong performance give him the edge at RB3 and did Behren Morton 's poise in the second half force the Patriots' hand to keep him on the active roster as QB3? -- Mike Reiss 

 Next game : at Cleveland Browns (Thursday, 8 p.m. ET, Prime Video)

 

 

 Eagles : Who will back up QB Jalen Hurts this season? Andy Dalton has started both preseason games -- seemingly an indication that he is ahead in the competition with Tanner McKee  to be Hurts' backup, despite the two splitting practice reps with the second team this summer. Dalton has not fared well in those games, however, going 3-of-10 for 44 yards against the Patriots and 3-of-6 for 20 yards versus the Baltimore Ravens .

 McKee tossed two touchdown passes against New England and was more efficient overall. But neither QB has clearly separated from the other, making for an interesting decision as the time nears to trim the roster to 53. -- Tim McManus 

 Next game : at Cincinnati Bengals (Friday, 8 p.m. ET, CBS)

 

 Bucs 16, Chiefs 15 
 

 Bucs: Has Jalon Daniels worked his way into the QB2 role behind Baker Mayfield ? Every time the undrafted free agent rookie out of Kansas has entered games, he has given the offense a jolt. He went 9-for-14 for 71 passing yards, including a 2-yard touchdown pass across his body to tight end Ko Kieft . Daniels also rushed for 23 yards and led a second scoring drive after Roman Parodie 's interception that was capped by a 1-yard Sean Tucker touchdown run. Then, Daniels went with a hard count on third-and-1 and lured the Chiefs offsides. His play on the move really stood out during a night when Jake Browning was pressured on 58% of his dropbacks and was sacked three times. -- Jenna Laine 

 Next game : at  Jacksonville Jaguars  (Friday, 7:30 p.m. ET)

 

 

 Chiefs: Who will be the right tackle for Patrick Mahomes on opening night? The team invested most of training camp in preparing Kahlil Benson , the undrafted rookie from Indiana. Benson's performance Saturday, however, was quite disappointing. He struggled in pass protection, surrendering quick pressure to rookie Rueben Bain Jr . and a strip-sack to outside linebacker Anthony Nelson . At this point, the Chiefs likely move Benson to guard, where he played much better against the Los Angeles Rams last week. Jaylon Moore , a five-year veteran, hasn't been impressive, either. But Moore is likely the Chiefs' most ideal option. The only other possibility is Esa Pole , a second-year player who took snaps Saturday at left tackle with the second-team offense. -- Nate Taylor 

 Next game : at Seattle Seahawks  (Friday, 8 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited)

 

 Bengals 27, Bears 9 

 

 Bears : Who will be the Bears' left tackle? The Bears are still searching for their starting left tackle and got an extended look at Braxton Jones and Theo Benedet in Cincinnati. After missing more than a week because of injury, Jones got back in the mix, and it feels like this is his job to lose, particularly after Jedrick Wills Jr . and Kiran Amegadjie were moved to right tackle. Until Ozzy Trapilo can participate fully in team reps while working his way off the PUP list, Jones and his 44 starts might give the Bears the best option for the consistency the coaches are seeking at the position. It took Chicago until cut-down day to name their Week 1 starter last year. The coaches hope that the Bears will have their answer earlier this year. -- Courtney Cronin 

 Next game : at Tennessee Titans (Saturday, 6 p.m. ET, NFL Network)

 

 Bengals: Has Dohnte Meyers done enough to seal a roster spot? He played extensively as a receiver and returner, and he was effective while he was on the field. He could be an option over Charlie Jones , who is competing for his spot despite being one of the best returners in the NFL. And secondly ...

 Do the Bengals have a viable swing tackle? Jalen Rivers and Javon Foster held down the edges of the offensive line to start the game. Cincinnati will need to solidify that spot ahead of Week 1. -- Ben Baby 

 Next game : at Philadelphia Eagles (Friday, 8 p.m. ET, CBS)

 

 Giants 26, Dolphins 3  

 

 Giants: What will New York do at wide receiver with Odell Beckham Jr . and Co.? Beckham is clearly on the bubble. Malik Nabers , Darnell Mooney and Braxton Berrios  all had the day off in Saturday's preseason game against the Dolphins. Malachi…

title: New NFL blocking, pass rush win rate formulas and takeaways
summary: After eight years, ESPN tweaked the formula for pass rush win rate and pass block win rate. What's new for 2026? Which players saw their stats impacted the most?
full_text:
Eight years after ESPN first launched its pass block and pass rush win rate statistics, they are both getting an upgrade.

 Win rates held up well considering they were the first NFL player-tracking metrics that ESPN created. But we've learned a lot -- and watched a ton of Micah Parsons pass-rush wins -- in the interim and have now implemented a bit of a facelift entering the 2026 NFL season . The result? Significant improvement in stability and reliability.

 ESPN sports data scientist Brian Burke explained the changes that we've made below, and analytics writer Seth Walder outlined five storylines that have surfaced with the tweaks.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Changes | Storylines 

 
 

 Burke: What's different? 
 The metrics generally work the same as they always have. They treat the pass rush and protection with a weak-link survival systems approach. The survival aspect means time is an essential factor -- winning a block at 2.0 seconds is very different than at 4.0 seconds. The " weak-link " aspect applies to the team/unit level, meaning any single pass-block loss on a play triggers a loss for the entire unit. After all, it really doesn't matter if there are four solid blocks and one failed block -- it only takes a single successful pass rusher to dramatically affect a play.

 A rusher generally triggers a win when his tracking chips are closer to the QB than those of his blocker(s). Win rates track the blocks throughout the duration of the play, creating a survival curve for any player or unit. For simplicity, we made 2.5 seconds after the snap the baseline for win rates, a reasonably representative single number that's easier to communicate than full curves at each time step. Think of win rates as a batting average for linemen.

 

 The most notable addition this season is the inclusion of a "bull rush win," when a defender pushes his blocker close enough to the QB to affect his vision or ability to step up, or forces him out of the pocket. The pass rusher might not get his tracking chips past his blocker's chips, but he successfully disrupted the play. We are confident that our definition of a bull rush win is useful. Just like for the legacy "chips past your blockers by 2.5 seconds" rule, plays with a bull win have a dramatically lower completion percentage, yards per attempt and EPA per play.

 In addition to bull rushes, we've made other improvements, such as fixing false positives from outside speed rushes when the rusher is never really a threat to the pocket, therefore refining the way blocks are defined and identified. These improvements have resulted in solid increases in year-over-year reliability. To the degree any metric measures personal skill, you would expect it to correlate with any single player from one year to the next. Reliability correlations increased from 0.53 for the legacy metrics to 0.59 for the new formulation. These are solid numbers as far as sports metrics go -- for context, MLB batting averages have between 0.4 to 0.5 year-to-year reliability.

 The legacy win rates correlated with EPA per play at 0.24, meaning that the metrics could account for about a quarter of the outcome of any play. The new version correlates at 0.34, accounting for about a third of the play outcome. This is a substantial amount, given everything else that affects a pass play -- including the QB, receivers and pass coverage, not to mention old-fashioned sample error.

 Win rate correlation with EPA also compares favorably to competing benchmark metrics. It's important to note that win rates do not see the outcome of the play by design. They can't cheat and know whether there was a sack or if the QB escaped pressure to throw a heroic touchdown. They're intended to isolate individual line play from everything else that's happening.

 

 The new formulation also addresses some past criticisms of win rates. They now identify chip blocks, both in terms of which pass rushers get chipped the most and which tackles get the most chip help. They also classify defensive stunts such as twists and simulated pressure. While we don't adjust the core win rate metrics for these factors, we will report them alongside the metrics the same way we've done with double-teams.

 

 Walder: Five win rate storylines to watch 
 

 1. Nick Herbig is still good in PRWR ... but no longer elite 
 Herbig has fascinated me for years because of his pass rush win rate prowess (26.3% in 2025, No. 1 in the NFL) combined with the Steelers' apparent hesitation to play him more. Part of the disconnect is that Herbig perhaps benefited disproportionately from the weak points of the old pass rush win rates metric -- high outside speed rushes when a defender gets too vertical to the point where he's not a threat to the quarterback even if he passes his blocker.

 The removal of these wins dropped Herbig's pass rush win rate at edge more than any other player. In the updated metric, Herbig's pass rush win rate at edge is 14.3% -- 14th best at the position. That's above average and well worth the big contract the Steelers gave him this offseason. But it is not elite territory; he's no longer competing with Packers edge rusher Micah Parsons at the top of the board. Broncos edge  Nik Bonitto , meanwhile, dropped from third (23.5%) to 10th (15.4%) at the position in the new version.

 What about in the other direction? Some big gainers included free agent  Joey Bosa , the Lions'  Aidan Hutchinson and the Commanders'  Odafe Oweh -- who each ranked in the top five in pass rush win rate at edge last season. The most surprising is Bosa, a 31-year-old former star. What changed for him? More than anything else, the metric's improved requirements about proximity to the quarterback shifted several of his previously designated losses into wins. Check out the top 10 at both edge and defensive tackle:

 

 

 
 

 2. Who won the most with bull rushes? 
 Bull rush wins were undercounted before, which has been corrected in the updated version. So, we can now see the value of power rushing more clearly.

 Bull rush wins are much more rare than traditional get-past-your-blocker pass-rush wins, and they're actually more valuable. The chance of a sack on a play featuring a bull rush win increases by eight percentage points (compared to six for all pass-rush wins). Even when the defense doesn't get home, the effect is large. Offenses average 6.3 yards per pass attempt on plays without a bull rush win to 5.0 with one.

 So, which players stand out for their bull-rushing ability? No one had more bull rush wins than Seahawks defensive tackle  Leonard Williams ' 18 last season, followed by Titans defensive tackle  Jeffery Simmons ' 16. Both players' overall pass rush win rate at defensive tackle increased with the change in the formula.

 Lions defensive tackle Alim McNeill recorded the highest bull rush win rate -- as in, bull rush wins per pass rush -- among players with at least 200 pass rushes.

 
 

 3. Who was chipped the most? 
 No player was chipped more often last season than Steelers edge rusher  T.J. Watt , who was chipped on 24.2% of his pass rushes -- well ahead of the Rams'  Myles Garrett , who finished second at 21.9%. They were followed by Browns edge  Alex Wright (21.4%), Texans edge  Will Anderson Jr . (20.9%) and Cowboys edge  Rashan Gary (20.2%).

 But does that explain Watt's down 2025, when his 10.1% pass rush win rate at edge ranked only 33rd? Not quite. Because when we look at percentage of plays when edge rushers were chipped or double-teamed, Watt no longer stands out, finishing 12th among edges (36.6%). Parsons easily commanded the most attention when combining the two, getting chipped or doubled on 54.0% of pass rushes, with Garrett finishing second at 46.1%. Parsons and Garrett ended up finishing first and fifth, respectively, in pass rush win rate at edge, well ahead of Watt.

title: 2026 San Francisco 49ers training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from 49ers training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. 49ers reporter Nick Wagoner has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at 49ers camp. What does  Mike Evans  look like as a top receiver on the 49ers? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the 49ers' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp previews for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from 49ers' camp 
 
 Shanahan dismisses idea RB McCaffrey sitting out for new deal 
 Can the 49ers depend on rookie WR De'Zhaun Stribling? 
 49ers' Ricky Pearsall has knee surgery, targets 9-month recovery 
 How the 49ers' defense looks different under Raheem Morris 
 Kyle Shanahan nears full strength, plans to coach preseason opener 
 Kittle eyes opener in Australia 
 

 

 Saturday, Aug. 22 
 Wide receiver Mike Evans was back at practice Saturday after leaving last Tuesday's session early with quad tightness. The Niners weren't concerned about it at the time and suggested Evans would be back soon, so his presence wasn't a total surprise.

 Evans went on to have a nice practice, connecting with QB Brock Purdy a few times for big gains and catching a short touchdown pass from Purdy in the red zone. RB Christian McCaffrey , meanwhile, did not return to practice from his own bout with tightness -- but he was seen in the weight room going through a workout.

 More observations: 

 
 Coach Kyle Shanahan is basically all the way back to full duties from his car accident, but he took another step Saturday when he was seen calling in plays on the walkie-talkie. It's the first time I've noticed it in this camp (doesn't mean it hasn't happened before), and he didn't do it the whole time, but it is also a sign that the regular season is fast approaching. 
 WR De'Zhaun Stribling and CB Deommodore Lenoir did not practice because of shoulder issues. They're considered day-to-day, according to the team. 
 The Niners welcomed back three potential important contributors from injury Saturday: RB Jordan James (rib), G Dominick Puni (concussion) and DT C.J. West (concussion). WR Malik Turner was also back in the mix, though he did some work on the side after individual. 
 Among the others not practicing after suffering injuries in Thursday's preseason game: LB Nick Martin (hamstring), CB Renardo Green (hamstring) and OL Austen Pleasants (knee). 
 James and rookie RB Kaelon Black have fresh legs and it shows after their returns from injury. Black, in particular, showed off some sure hands in the pass game, one of the questions surrounding him coming out of the draft. 
 Other 49ers I did not see participating today who haven't had any injuries disclosed: LB Jalen Graham , WR Wesley Grimes (was seen with a wrap on his hand), RB Zamir White and DL Xavier Thomas . 
 

 

 
 Tuesday, Aug. 18 
 EL SEGUNDO, Calif. -- The 49ers' offense largely had its way with the Titans in a joint practice last week, but that was far from the case against the Chargers.

 The unit started well, as rookie running back Kaelon Black broke some big runs early. But the Chargers settled in for the second half and made life hard on QB Brock Purdy & Co. in the move-the-ball, two-minute and red zone periods.

 Chargers linebacker  Del'Shawn Phillips  even picked off a Purdy pass intended for tight end  Luke Farrell when safety  Derwin James Jr . got his hand in the way and tipped it to him.

 All in all, it wasn't the most encouraging outing against another team that should be a playoff contender this season.

 "Obviously, there was some good stuff, some stuff we need to work on, but I just feel like they came out with a little more of a chip on their shoulder," Purdy said.

 More observations: 

 
 The 49ers and Chargers were all about their business with no notable skirmishes. That's unusual for a joint practice, and it led to Shanahan delivering the funniest line of the day as he poked fun at Robert Saleh, the Titans' coach and his good friend. Asked if there was a reason for the lack of fighting, Shanahan joked, "No, [the Chargers'] head coach has more discipline than Tennessee's." 
 Black was one of three 49ers to return to practice Tuesday, joining receiver  Demarcus Robinson (who only missed Sunday) and defensive lineman  Keion White . White and Black had been dealing with adductor injuries, though White did not finish the session. 
 Defensive tackle  C.J. West did not practice because of a concussion, which makes him the fifth player in this camp to have suffered a head injury. Defensive lineman  Titus Leo also had a concussion and was waived/injured Tuesday as the team brought back defensive tackle  Evan Anderson . 
 The competition for the backup running back job behind Christian McCaffrey has been difficult to handicap because of injuries to all of the primary contenders for that job. But Black picked up where he left off before his injury. He broke a long, possible touchdown run down the left side early in the session and clearly has the freshest legs of the bunch. 
 Chargers OLB  Tuli Tuipulotu  gave the Niners fits, particularly in the run game where he had at least three run stuffs. 
 WR  Mike Evans , who returned from a tight quad last week, took part in most of Tuesday's practice but stopped before the final periods. He initially had his left foot wrapped in ice before watching the end of the session with that ice pack relocated to his left quad. 
 
 
 

 Sunday, Aug. 16 
 49ers defensive end Nick Bosa hasn't practiced since Aug. 3. In fact, Bosa hadn't been spotted on the practice field doing work on the side since then. Until Sunday.

 Though Bosa, who has been battling soreness and tendinitis as he recovers from a torn ACL, did not return to practice, he went through an extensive workout on a side field. Niners coach Kyle Shanahan said Tuesday that Bosa is dealing with "a pretty normal thing with ACLs," but given Bosa's injury history and that he was practicing before the soreness, it seemed to be a setback.

 "We have to be smart here from week to week," Shanahan said. "But no concerns about him."

 Though there are still hurdles to clear before Bosa returns to practice, Sunday was, at minimum, a notable step forward.

 More observations: 

 
 Three 49ers were added to the nonparticipant list Sunday: G Dominick Puni is in concussion protocol, defensive tackle Gracen Halton has an ankle injury and WR Demarcus Robinson missed the session for undisclosed reasons. 
 DT C.J. West and DE Titus Leo were hurt on back-to-back plays during a team drill. Both limped to the locker room and did not return. 
 WR  Deebo Samuel Sr . and WR Jacob Cowing were also shaken up at various points but returned and finished the session. 
 QB Kurtis Rourke did not practice again after he left last week's preseason opener because of breathing trouble. It's unclear what his injury is, but OC Klay Kubiak indicated that Rourke won't be out long. 
 With Puni out, Robert Jones worked at right guard as Jones, Connor Colby and Carver Willis continue to push for the starting left guard job. 
 Undrafted rookie DT James Thompson Jr . has been an under-the-radar surprise in camp and got some extra looks with the starters after West went down. 
 CB Renardo Green took issue with an official after he was whistled for a couple of penalties in red zone work. He got a flag for defensive pass interference then one for defensive holding. When he successfully defended a third pass thrown his way, he asked the official why he didn't throw a third flag.
